title: Early thinking about the composition of matter
competency: Give a short history of the atom and compare the continuous and discrete theories of matter.

keywords.def: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
A very small particle; the building block of all substances.
Aristotle's idea: matter can be divided forever, with no smallest particle.
Democritus' idea: there is a limit to dividing matter; it is made of atoms.

en.text: Ancient Greek thinkers argued about matter. Aristotle said matter is continuous: you can divide it forever. Democritus said matter is discrete: dividing must stop at tiny, uncuttable particles he called atomos, atoms.

am.text: ዲሞክሪተስ ቁስ አካል ሊከፋፈሉ የማይችሉ ጥቃቅን ቅንጣቶች (አቶሞች) እንዳሉት ተናግሯል። አርስቶትል ደግሞ ቁስ ያለገደብ ይከፋፈላል ብሏል።

screens.title: Cut it again and again
screens.ask: You cut a piece of chalk in half, then in half again, again and again. What happens in the end?
opts: You reach tiny pieces that cannot be cut any more
screens.after: Greek thinkers argued about this 2400 years ago! Democritus said you reach tiny particles, atoms. Aristotle said you can cut forever. Today we know matter is made of atoms, so Democritus was closer.
screens.best: You reach tiny pieces that cannot be cut any more

screens.title: Activity 2.2: keep halving the chalk
screens.note: Start with a 10 mm (1 cm) piece. 1 mm = 1 000 000 nm. An atom is about 0.1–0.5 nm wide. After about 25 cuts, the piece would be as small as one atom.

screens.title: What is matter made of?
paras: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
The earliest discussion of the structure of matter comes from ancient Greek philosophers.
Some argued matter is continuous: it can be divided endlessly.
Others believed matter is discrete: it cannot be divided forever.
screens.note: The definition of matter is added; the book asks it in Activity 2.1.

people.name: Democritus
people.did: Said all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atomos ("uncuttable"). Matter is discrete.

people.name: Aristotle
people.did: Said matter can be divided forever. He thought matter was made of fire, earth, air and water. Matter is continuous.

table: There is a limit to breaking matter

screens.title: Table 2.1 as a picture: two answers to one question
sets: Discreteness theory. There is a limit to breaking matter. Believed in atoms.
Continuous theory. Matter is infinitely divisible. Rejected atoms; matter is fire, earth, air and water.
overlaps: Ancient Greek philosophers. Both asked: what is matter made of?

screens.title: Key words
defs: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
A very small particle; the building block of all substances.
Aristotle's idea: matter can be divided forever, with no smallest particle.
Democritus' idea: there is a limit to dividing matter; it is made of atoms.

screens.text: Early ideas about matter: who first proposed the idea of atoms?
screens.why:
Democritus said matter is made of tiny particles.
He called them atomos, which means uncuttable.
Aristotle rejected atoms.
Dalton came more than 2000 years later.
So the answer is Democritus.

screens.text: Early ideas about matter: the idea that matter is continuous was proposed by
screens.why:
Continuous means it can be divided forever.
Aristotle argued that division never stops.
He rejected the idea of atoms.
Democritus said the opposite: matter is discrete.
So the answer is Aristotle.

screens.text: Two theories of matter: sort each statement under the right theory.
items: There is a limit to breaking matter
Matter is fire, earth, air and water
screens.why:
Discreteness theory (Democritus): there is a limit to breaking matter, and atoms exist.
Continuous theory (Aristotle): matter is infinitely divisible.
Aristotle also believed matter is fire, earth, air and water.

screens.ask: Word meaning: the Greek word atomos means ___
screens.why:
Democritus gave the tiny particles a name.
Atomos means "uncuttable" or "indivisible".
He believed they were the smallest pieces of matter.
So the answer is uncuttable.
screens.clue: It tells you what you cannot do to an atom.

screens.text: Then and now: today we know atoms exist and are made of even smaller particles. Which old idea was closer to the truth?
opts: Democritus: matter is made of tiny particles
screens.ans: Democritus: matter is made of tiny particles
screens.why:
Matter is made of atoms, as Democritus said.
So matter does not divide forever: Aristotle was wrong there.
But atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.
So atoms are not truly uncuttable.
Democritus was closer, but not exactly right.

items.text: Exercise 2.1, comparing theories: how are the two theories alike?
opts: Both are ancient Greek ideas about the structure of matter
Both say matter is made of atoms
items.ans: Both are ancient Greek ideas about the structure of matter
items.why:
Both come from ancient Greek philosophers.
Both try to answer one question: what is matter made of?
They give different answers about dividing matter.
Only the discreteness theory says atoms exist.
items.clue: Who proposed them, and about what?

items.text: Exercise 2.1, comparing theories: how are they different?
opts: One has a limit to dividing (atoms); the other has no limit
items.ans: One has a limit to dividing (atoms); the other has no limit
items.why:
Discreteness theory: dividing matter has a limit; you reach atoms.
Continuous theory: there is no limit and no atoms.
So one has a limit and the other has none.

test.text: Democritus' theory: according to Democritus, matter is
test.why:
Democritus believed in atoms.
Atoms are separate tiny particles.
Matter made of separate particles is called discrete.
So his answer is discrete.

test.text: Aristotle's theory: Aristotle believed matter was made of
test.why:
Aristotle rejected atoms.
He thought all matter was made of four things.
These were fire, earth, air and water.
Protons and molecules were unknown in his time.

test.text: Continuous theory, true or false: it rejected the idea of atoms.
test.why:
The continuous theory says matter can be divided forever.
If it divides forever, there is no smallest particle.
So there can be no atoms.
Table 2.1: it rejected the idea of atoms. True.

test.text: Two theories of matter: "There is a limit to which matter is broken" belongs to
test.why:
A limit means you reach a smallest piece.
That smallest piece is the atom.
The theory with atoms is the discreteness theory.
The continuous theory says there is no limit.

test.text: Aristotle's view: which statement would Aristotle agree with?
opts: You can always cut a piece in half again
test.ans: You can always cut a piece in half again
test.why:
Aristotle followed the continuous theory.
It says matter can be divided forever.
So you can always cut a piece in half again.
The other options talk about atoms, which he rejected.
